WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill (No. 88) to provide for the appointment of a Tariff Commission.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister).
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Hear, hear.
My hon. friends applaud the sentiment. The sentiment is embodied in the amendment, and yet they propose to vote down that amendment.
Come again.

There is no difficulty about that. This principle seems to require a few -words from myself because the opposite position, which has been so well established through the mouth of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), was perhaps given more definite expression to by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) in the speech which he made and in which he referred to some remarks of my own. But, I should like to point out before referring specifically to that speech what is the origin of this whole commission, and what is the bearing of the amendment upon the efficiency of the commission. The country ought to appreciate the fact that the proposition for this commission originated some years ago with the Manufacturers' Association of Canada. They carried a resolution at one of their meetings in favour of this very thing, and they used in regard to it-and this is very significant language-that we ought to take the tariff out of politics. That means, as I have proved at previous stages of the debates upon this Bill, taking the taxing power out of the hands of the people if it means anything at all. It reminds me of the story of a deacon in a darky church within the poultry belt who went to the pastor of the church after^ he had preached a sermon, and said to him: We wish you to understand that what we want you to do is to preach religion pure and undefiled and keep out of the chicken
coop business. _ Our friends opposite are voting on politics pure and undefiled, and they do not want us to give any attention to a commission which is outside of the ordinary parliamentary procedure altogether. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) said in the later stages of the_ debate upon this measure that he believed that this measure would be very favourable to the farmers and consumers.
I am sure he will not contradict me if I quote his language to that effect. I want the House to connect that language of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance with the language of my hon. friend the member for Brantford. I was mentioned playfully, of course, as a possible candidate for membership on the Tariff Commission. I need not say that I was not an applicant nor do I consider myself in line for any appointment under this government. What my hon. friend objects to is the very thought that any free trader should be upon the Tariff Commission, because, forsooth, he said that he was a gun which would not go off. My hon. friend, who has had an intimate connection with the Manufacturers' Association, wants to shoot somebody. While I may have been a gun of some kind, was my hon. friend not afraid that if I did by any chance go off I would possibly shoot into the ranks of the manufacturers? He was not concerned about the gun going off or not going off if I were a member of the commission, but he was afraid that I would possibly like to shoot into the manufacturers ranks. Was not that the legitimate inference from that language, was not that the meaning behind the words of my hon. friend? Was it not that this commission is by no means expected to touch the sacrosanct manufacturers, but if it does not touch them my hon. friend might shoot some one. Is he going to shoot the farmers and consumers of this country on behalf of the Manufacturers' Association? I invite the Minister of Finance to reconcile his language about this being a benefit to the farmers and consumers with the evident intention of one of his followers that this proposition should not benefit them but that it may possibly have the effect of shooting into the ranks of a large body of the people of this country. I apologize for detaining the House at this stage of the [DOT] business, but 1 think that these words used by the hon. gentleman are of sufficient importance to justify me in rising even if I have delayed the debate for a few moments.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clark, Red Deer) what he means by saying that I was very closely associated with the Manufacturers' Association.
If there was any offence in those words I gladly withdraw them. I understand my hon. friend has been a manufacturer, and the probability is that he had a close connection with that association.

The statement of the hon. gentleman is that I was very closely associated with the Manufacturers' Association. The imputation is that I was an officer or member of the association. Does he say that now?
Oh, no, I gladly withdraw it if it is an offence.
There is nothing to withdraw if the hon. gentleman did not make the- statement.
I withdraw it if it is in the least degree offensive to my [DOT] hon. friend.

My attention has been called to the first subclause of section 107 under tire heading of ' Spring Wheat/ which says:
No. 1 Manitoba Hard wheat shall he sound and well cleaned, weighing not less than 60 pounds to the bushel, and ehall he composed of at least 75 per cent of hard Red Fife wheat.
I have before me a resolution, a copy of which was'sent to the hon. minister, in which it was pointed out that the wordis ' well cleaned ' are a hardship, because dockage is now put upon those who sell grain, which is not well cleaned, so that a person who is selling hard wheat which might otherwise grade as No. 1, if it is not cleaned as required by the Act, suffers a double loss-a loss both in grade and in dockage. This resolution points out that justice would be done if the same wording were used as is used with regard to No. 2 Manitoba Northern wheat, and if we used the words "reasonably cleaned ' instead of the words ' well cleaned.' It is pointed out that farmers have not facilities for cleaning well, and that all that they can be expected to do is to clean reasonably. I hope the minister will consider that point.

The matter was considered when we were passing over these grades. Not only was it considered in conjunction with the deputation from the northwest who were here, but it has been considered later in conjunction with the inspector himself. There are objections urged against the suggested change in the quality of this grade. The words ' reasonably cleaned ' involve a doubt. A man who is inspecting knows when a grade is well 'Cleaned; that is easily apparent. To say that he must see that it is reasonably well cleaned leaves it open to the interpretation of various inspectors in a different way 'from what it would be if the actual definition were made. That is with reference to the best quality of our wheat, and if any grade of wheat should he raised and kept to a. high standard, it is that grade. The same words are used with reference to No. 1 Hard Fife and No. 1 Manitoba Northern, and it is not until you come to the lower grade of wheat that the words ' reasonably cleaned ' are used instead of the words ' well cleaned.' I can see the point that my hon. friend makes; but this grade should be high, and when it passes out from inspection, it should be well Mr. OLIVER.
cleaned. If there are variations in the wheat itself, as to what is mixed with it, the dockage will always be in proportion to the lamoumt of material for which dockage is allowed. If the wheat is reasonably clean, more dockage will toe taken than if it is well cleaned. I do not see where the [DOT]seller stands to lose in that respect. He does not want to get a price for the grain unless it is up to a certain standard and unless it is well cleaned. There will be a heavier dockage for wheat which is partially cleaned and a lighter dockage for that which is better cleaned.

I do not like to press this matter on the minister under, the circumstances, but I think really it is important to have some change made at the present stage. In the province of Saskatchewan, at least in that part where I reside, we have experimented for some time with wheat. I myself have been growing Preston for a number of years, and as a matter of fact the Act as *it stands now is a dead letter so far as shutting out that wheat is concerned. I sell it year by year and it passes just the same as Red Fife.
A twin sister to it.
I think that so far as quality is concerned we suffer no injury.
Do you sell on sample?

Not on sample, we sell on grade, and I have had it repeatedly graded as No. 1 and 2 Northern, that is pure Preston with not a bit of Red Fife in it as far as I could tell, and bearded wheat too. That is done in actual practice without much damage resulting, but it does not look quite right to my mind that there should be a provision in bur Act which the inspectors either wink at, or are unable to carry out. Preston and Marquis are the varieties of grain which I am more accustomed to. I fancy that an expert can tell at almost any time the difference between Preston and Red Fife more by the shape of the grain than anything else. But still they ipass it continually as No. 1 and No. 2 Northern, and it is quite just that they should do so I think. I do not know tliat the tests have shown the Preston to be quite as good a wheat as the Red Fife, but it is so very near it that! there is not a material difference. The Marquis also can be distinguished from the Red Fife, while the Preston is a longer and thinner grain than the Red Fife I think the Marquis on the other hand is a little thicker, and possibly a little shorter and of a deeper red. But the tests so far as they have been applied

show the Marquis to be as good a grain as the Red Fife, or a little better from a flour-making standpoint. I do not wish to press this matter too far but I thought it necessary to tell the minister what I have seen myself; and while, as I say, there may be no very great injury to the farmer, I a?n not sure that to have a law which is virtually ignored is a very good thing. We either ought not to permit our officials to wink at and ignore the Act, or we ought to change the law.
I have grown the Stanley and have found n,o difficulty in selling it, though I think I only grew it one year. But I know that the Stanley is continually being passed as Red Fife. I presume the same applies to the Marquis.
Can the grain buyers tell the difference?
I think if I were a grain buyer I could tell the difference between the Preston and Red Fife.
Could tlhe average grain buyers in the West detect the difference?

I think so. The, Preston is longer and a somewhat thinner grain than the Red Fife. But I think it is practically as hard. There is a marked difference between the Maxquid and the Red Fife, at least a difference that can be seen.
How many years have they been experimenting with the Marquis ?

It cannot have been for very long, seeing that it is being sold at $12 a bushel. That may not be true with regard to the Marquis just now, but, even though frozen it is sold at $2, $3, and $4 a bushel. So, there is no danger, at present because none of it will be sold in the ordinary way.
It will practically all be sold for seed ?

Yes. No one who has Marquis will sell it except for seed, unless it is altogether too dirty.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the House to the Marconigraph service that has been Mr. THOMSON (Qu'Appelle).
established between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands. I have on two occasions asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) if it was true that news was being supplied by the government to the Magdalen Islands during the season when navigation is closed. And I was answered yesterday that tlhe Postmaster General had established a news service and that this service had begun last week.
Some years ago, I obtained from the Minister of Public Works a condensed cable news service for the fishermen and1 merchants of the Magdalen Islands, giving them the state of the fish-markets and of staples generally at Halifax and Pictou. That news was cabled from Meat Cove to the islands. But I never asked for the supply of political news to the islands. The service of the cable was also given to the islanders at a cheap rate in order to give them the necessary facilities for communicating with their relatives on the mainland. This year when the estimates of the Public Works Department came before the House, on the item of telegraph lines in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, I called the attention of the Minister of Public Works to that service established through my instrumentality a few years ago. To my astonishment I learned the other day that a more extended' service of news had been granted by the government to the islands. I immediately suspected something, and my suspicions were right. I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), what was the nature of this service, and was answered yesterday by the Postmaster General' (Mr. Pelletier), that that service was non-political. Well, Sir, I hold1 in my hand the first instalment of news which was sent by the political editor in Quebec to the Magdalen Islands. And I must protest against it. No political leader has the right to use the moneys of the people to supply partisan news to one section of the country at the expense of the whole country. This first instalment is to be followed by weekly letters to the Magdalen Islands. I shall not worry the House by reading these despatches, but I see one paragraph here which deals with the G.T.P. contract which was interpreted by the Privy Council the other day. And the whole statement is biased, and is given from the Conservative point of view only. I need1 hardly mention other paragraphs in which eulogies and encomiums are heaped upon the head of the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), in connection with Quebec public expenditures. I call the attention of the acting leader of the House (Mr. Foster), to this state of affairs. The question will be brought up again in the House, but, meantime, he should warn

his colleagues that they must not expect the country to pay for partisan news wired to the Magdalen Islands under the excuse of giving to the islanders something of the news of the ou'tside world.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux), give us a specimen of this partisanship?
Just before my hon. friend read's, would he kindly state from what he is reading?

From the Toronto Daily ' Star,' which publishes the first instalment of news sent to the Magdalen Islands. It has been published1 in .other newspapers, but I happen to have the Toronto 4 Star ' in my hands, and from this I read.	,
My hon. friend is certain that that is the pure, undiluted news that was sent to the Magdalen Islands?
I am morally convinced that these are the items of news sent to the islands.
It is very important to know that it is really so.

Very well. I will take the hint of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster). I will put a 'question in the order paper or move a motion asking the Postmaster General to give the House an exact copy of the news which was sent from Quebec to the Magdalen Islands. And I shall defer my remarks to another day. But I again state that if the facts are as mentioned in the Toronto 4 Star,' it is simply an abuse of the confidence of parliament, and it is a gross abuse of the privileges enjoyed by a minister of the Crown. He has
no right to use the money of the people to supply partisan news to one section of the country.

There are complaints throughout the lower provinces that the rolling stock is not up to the standard, either in quantity or quality. It is said that in order to get a surplus these considerations are being neglected. Has the minister looked into that question?
As I said last night, we are taking stock to arrive at a conclusion. Later on we will find in the estimates an item for cars and rolling stock.

I would like to ask the minister if he will take into consideration the advisability of retaining this surplus in some way for a special fund, and using it towards renewing rolling stock, bridges and whatever else is necessary. I know I am opening up a big question. I am not finding any fault, because my own party friends have erred to the same extent that his friends did when they were in power, and I am afraid that my hon. friend may err in the future. There is a wide difference between the Intercolonial railway and any ordinary railway company. I realize that railway companies are in the habit of charging many items to capital, and justly. If this method of bookkeeping has been adopted on the Intercolonial in the past, to some extent we are following the principles of railway companies. But there is a vast difference between the two. The Intercolonial is an asset of Canada, and it is a necessity to the maritime provinces. It is a great advantage, not only to the maritime provinces but to Quebec and Ontario as well; because while it is true that we have a reasonable freight rate and passenger rate, yet the great part of that advantage inures to the benefit I think of the manufacturers and producers of Ontario and Quebec, certainly to a much greater extent than to the consumers of the maritime provinces. Now the trouble comes in that when we have a surplus of $600,000 or $700,000, as we are to have this year, that goes into the ordinary fund of Canada, and the people of the maritime provinces, or the Intercolonial railway, get no credit for it whatever. It simply swells the revenue of Canada, and it is taken to be used in other portions of Canada-I am not saying it is not properly used, but the difficulty comes in that if unfortunately there comes a year when there is a deficit, then there is a great cry goes up from the rest of Canada that the Intercolonial is a burden, it is something that ought not to be allowed. Several times since I have been in parliament I have heard this cry go up: The Intercolonial is not paying its way; therefore it is going Mr. COCHRANE.
to be sold, or given away to some company, or something of that kind.
If this money were placed in a special fund, out of which betterments could be paid for, we would at least have the satisfaction of knowing whether the Intercolonial railway is paying its way or not. I submit that there has been hardly a year since the Intercolonial railway has been in existence when the people of Canada have been able to tell by reading the report of the minister, or the blue-books, whether the Intercolonial railway has paid its way or not. Possibly I am breaking in on new ground; I know that I am voicing something which has been opposed to the policy of my friends, but I think I am talking common sense, and I am appealing to the minister, not to give me his decision now, but to take this matter into his consideration. Take the figures which the minister gave me last evening; he says that we have a surplus this year of something like $600,000 or $700,000, but that we spent last year a million and a half on capital account. It seems to me that where entirely new rolling stock is obtained, additional locomotives and cars, it is proper to charge the cost of these to capital account. Where rolling stock has been worn out and new cars are obtained to take their place then it is proper to charge the cost of the new cars to revenue or operating expenses. I understand that where a bridge has been replaced by a heavier bridge, owing to the necessity of providing for heavier locomotives, the difference between what would have been the fair value of the bridge that was replaced and the cost of the new bridge has been charged to capital account. Every railway company does that. I have been told by a gentleman connected with the Canadian Pacific railway that since that road wa3 supposed to be entirely constructed and completed the Canadian Pacific railway has expended more on capital account, in rebuilding, improving grades, laying heavier rails and rebuilding bridges than the original cost of the road. Most of us are business men to some extent and if, in my business, or in any of the enterprises with which I am connected, I kept taking money out of earnings and paying it out in the form of dividends, and if I was issuing new stock to keep the thing going, possibly I myself might get some money out of the dividend, but I would not be creating very much of a property to hand down to my successors.

This is a letter from, the former Minister of Railways to Mr, Swan, the president of the Salisbury and Harvey Railway Company:
Office of the Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa, Aug. 2, 1911.
Dear Sir,-The policy of the Dominion government, as announced, is to take such lines as may, in the interests of the public, furnish branch lines to the Intercolonial railway. At the session of parliament just closed a Bill was introduced naming the basis on which these lines might be taken over. This Bill got its first reading, and was under discussion in Committee of the Whole House when dissolution took place.
In the meantime, the owners of these lines made representations that the basis could not be worked out practically, and after consultation with the Minister of Railways another basis was proposed, which does not seem unreasonable.
I have your offer to sell outright the Salisbury and Harvey railway, with its extensions and rolling stock for ($120,000) one hundred and twenty thousand dollars. Ordinarily I would not at the present moment make a proposition respecting- the taking over of this line, were it not that some nineteen miles of the road are not now open for traffic, and the people who were accustomed to. a railway service are suffering a great injustice and hardship, so that I feel strong steps should he taken to remedy this situation.
The government is prepared, therefore, to propose to you that at the coming session of parliament they will introduce legislation, either to take over the road at one hundred and twenty thousand ($120,000) or to take it over on the basis recently arrived at after consultation between the owners of the various branch lines and the Minister of Railways on condition that you will agree, at once-to make sufficient repairs to the line to enable it to be operated and begin at once to operate it over its entire length for the convenience of the public. Such repairs to be made under the supervision of the Railway Department.
Should parliament approve of the government taking over this line, the amount of money expended by yon in such repairs will either be added to the sale price, or to the capital on which you will he paid interest under the rental basis.
Kindly let me hear from you without delay as the people complain loudly of the inconvenience.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) GEORGE P. GRAHAM.
A. S. Swan, Esq.,
President, Salisbury and Harvey Railway, Hillsborough, N.B.

We will wait a while, just as long as my hon. friend wants, but let us wait, do not let us anticipate what may be discovered, do not throw out insinuations as to what may be discovered, do not seek to poison the public mind with respect to the administration of a department until matters are brought out, if there are any that can be brought out, reflecting on the administration of the department. It seems to me that is only fair, only what any public man administering a department has a right to expect from political opponents whether they are members of this House or outsiders.
My hon. friend has complained of delay by the late government in making provision for the opening of this railway. It seems to me my hon. friend speaks in that respect without consideration. This is a private road, owned by a private company which received subsidies rrom the provincial government and1 from the Dominion government. It did cease to operate a portion of its line. Very great complaints were made by the people, the very strongest possible complaint was made by the late representative of Kings and Albert, and at the earnest solicitation of Dr. McAllister and representatives from other constituencies in which railways were in a somewhat similar position, the late government asked parliament to enact a law of a very drastic character under which if a road ceased to be operated, proceedings might be taken for the sale of it in order to take the most effective measures possible to secure its being reopened and operated upon a safe and proper basis. But in this particular case the company said we have not the money to put this 20 miles in order, we cannot reopen it, unless we can get rails, we have not the means to procure rails, and we cannot do anything towards reopening the road unless the government will come to our rescue and give us a loan of rails pending the comple-

tion of an arrangement for taking over the various branch lines of railways. That was a very difficult thing to do, if a proposition like that were put up to the present Minister of Railways, he would say that was a question that required1 careful consideration.

How long did it take
to say all that? [DOT]
It has not taken me very long.
How long would it take for the people to make their statement, and for you to grant that relief? Would it take all the months that the road remained idle until the 1st of August?

It took a good deal of consideration on the part of the government before they would approve a recommendation which I made that the government should come to the rescue of this road, and make a loan of this large quantity of rails to them. It meant lending the company rails to relay 20 miles of road, it meant contracting quite a large indebtedness, and was a matter requiring very careful consideration, and the government very properly took quite a considerable time before deciding to do it. My hon. friend knows that another part of this railway extending to Alma was closed up by the Albert Railway Company.
Not the same company.
It may be another company, but a continuation of the line owned and operated by this company.
That had nothing to do with it.

And my hon. friend know's that the rails of that road were taken up and disposed of, and I think my hon. friend had something to do with the matter as solicitor or otherwise, and would know something about it.
I know all about it.

That was a piece of road which would have been a feeder to this part, which w.as aided by the late government and unfortunately it went out of service, the rails were taken up and that part ceased to be operated, thereby, of course, rendering the other part- of the road less profitable than it otherwise would have been. I submit that, the late government so far from 'being censurable for any delay which took place with regard to making a loan of these rails, were entitled to receive, *and did receive, from the people of Albert county, and should receive from my hon. friend as their representative, heiarty thanks in respect of the matter, because what the State government agreed to do was
of great public service and it affords me the greatest pleasure to know that tire present Minister of Railways has carried out what we agreed to do.
One word with regard to what my horn, friend says was 'the improper advice which I gave to send 'forward these rails upon my receiving information that the contract had been signed. The hon. gentleman says that this was a contract which was flying around loose somewhere. It was nothing of the kind. That draft of agreement had been brought to St. John by the law clerk of the department, its terms had been approved of by the deputy Minister of Justice, by the general manager of the Intercolonial railway, and 'by Mr. Raymond, solicitor of the 'Company, and all that remained was to take it to New York to secure its execution by the president of the company under the seal of the company, after which it was to be forwarded to the deputy Minister of Railways at Ottawa. I think it was not an imprudent thing to say to the deputy minister that it would be proper for him to have the rails loaded and sent forward, because in the ordinary course before those rails would reach tine BsunveyJSalisbury road, the contract would reach Ottawa, where it would be executed by the then Minister of Railways 'and the whole matter would be completed. The rails were so loaded that they were kept in the possession and under the control of the authorities of the Intercolonial railway until that agreement reached Ottawa, >and when there w.as inexplicable delay in its reaching Ottawa, when it was found that Mr. Raymond was for some reason delaying in sending it forward, the railway authorities acted very properly in issuing orders not to deliver the rails to the company because the agreement had not reached Ottawa. They acted entirely properly afterwards in waiting until the 26th of October under the present minister when the agreement was received, properly executed, when, without any thank's to the hon. member for Kings & Albert (Mr. Fowler), the present minister carried out the arrangement made by the late minister and ordered delivery of the rails.	-

I do not think my hon. friend has explained the long delay of almost a year during which this railway was down before action was taken on the 2nd of August by the government. The only explanation he has given is that he acted promptly and brought the matter before his colleagues. It took his colleagues a *long time to inform themselves as to whether or not he was correct in the statements he was making. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman's colleagues Should have had more confidence in 'the statements he made, and should not 'have required all thoise months of extra information outside

of what ihe was -able to give them, unless there was some very good reason, for it.
My hon. friend has referred to another road, which he says was a part of this, and has said that I had something to do with the disposal of the rails on that road. There was another road in the county, but it was no part of the Salisbury & Albert Railway. It was a road from Harvey to Alma. ' It has been in existence 1" or 18 years. The ties were all rotten, the bridges were all down, and the rails were being stolen by private parties. They supposed that the road had been abandoned, and they carried off the rails and used them for various purposes. Certain persons who were clients of my office had a judgment against the road, and the rails were sold under that judgment. Why does my hon. friend drag in that transaction? To draw a herring across the trail? I cannot understand what it has possibly to do with this railway.
Was it not all one continuous railway.
Not at all.
Was it not a continuous railway, although owned by two separate companies?

As a matter of fact there were three railways there-the Salisbury & Albert, the one under discussion, the Harvey branch connecting Albert with Harvey, under a different management, and the railway from Harvey to Alma, under different management and different ownership. It was the road from Harvey to Alma which was down all those years, nothing was left but the right of way and a portion of the rails. My hon. friend knew that perfectly well. He knew -that the Albert Southern, so-called, had nothing to do with the Harvey & Alma, and why he dragged it into the discussion I do not know. Did he want to cast some discredit on myself? I do not know why otherwise; and if that is all the argument that my hon. friend can put up for the long and cruel-and I say it advisedly-way of the late Government, it is a very lame and very poor defence, and it was so considered by the people of Albert county. Let me tell you that the people of Albert county are well pleased and well satisfied now with the result, and I may state that they give the credit to the present member for Kings and Albert for the redress of the great grievance under which the suffered for so many years.
It is not the first time that the people have been deceived, as my hon. friend says.
No. or my hon. friend would not be here.

Let me say, as the concluding remarks of this debate so far as 1 am concerned, that the people certainly have great reason to be satisfied with the policy which was inaugurated by the late government, of taking over the branch line railways, under which that government agreed to lend the rails to this Company in order to have the road improved, so that it could be put in good running condition, and which has been very properly carried out by the present Minister of Railways-I say that the people ought to be gratified that that policy has been brought to such a successful issue; and if my hon. friend is clever enough to make the people believe in a state of facts that does not exist, then he is cleverer than even those of us who have admiration for his intellect would give him the credit of being.

Let me say this, that the people are satisfied and gratified that there is to-day in power a government which does something more than promise. That was all that the late government did with regard to that constituency at any rate it dealt in empty promises. To-day we have a government that deals in performances.

I want to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways to the case of a young man in Nova Scotia named Joseph Benoit, who was dismissed by my hon. friend. He had been for a number of years an employee of the railway, and had.paid into the provident fund a considerable amount of money. He has called my attention to the fact that he has received an official letter informing him that he cannot receive back the amount of money which he has paid in. It does seem to me that that is very unfair, particularly in view of the law on the subject. Chapter 22 of the Acts of 1907 says that employees who are discharged from the service for any cause other than those mentioned in paragraph 'b' of section 17, after they have been three or more years contributors to the fund, may be paid out of the fund the total amount of their contributions to the fund, but without interest and less the cost and expenses of medical examinations. Paragraph 'b' of section 17 referred to is this:
Those who are discharged from the servioe on account, of wilful default, misconduct negligence in the performance of their duties, drunkenness, fraud or dishonesty.
A charge arising out of political interest does not come within the things mentioned in this paragraph.
Would not that be misconduct?

He is not charged with misconduct, but with political inter-

lerence, which is not misconduct in the sense of the statute, which relates to his conduct on duty or to any offence involving moral turpitude. Certainly it would be straining the construction of this statute very much to keep from this man the money which he has actually paid into this fund, and which was kept out of his wages, because he got interested in politics to an unusual extent. I would like the minister to look into this case and see that justice is done to this man. I am only asking my friend to carry out the statute.
I shall be very glad to look into it.

I have a similar case to bring to the attention of the hon. minister, though it is slightly different, inasmuch as the man tendered his resignation. The case is that of John Girrior, Tracadie, Antigonish county. He was section foreman, and had been in the employ of the department for upwards of 14 years. He was supposed to be a Liberal,
I understand, and some people got busy to put him out of the way. Then he received notice some time in October, after this government came into power, that he was no longer to act as foreman and another man who was under him was appointed in his place he however being continued as underman. The result was that Mr. Girrior, who lived about the middle of the section

being an under-man-had to walk to the end of the section every morning before 7 o'clock when the day's work begins. Now, unfortunately he had met with an accident and had his leg broken about a year ago in consequence of which rheumatism developed. The result was that it was very hard for him to walk from the middle to the end of his section in order to get to his work, as he was required to do, every morning at 7 o'clock.
How far would that be?

These sections are 6 or 7 miles in length and it would be half that distance. At any rate it was quite apparent to him in his way of thinking-whether rightly or wrongly-that this was a subterfuge, that he was degraded in the service to get him out of the way in order to make room for the man who was appointed as his successor. Therefore to save himself from the odium of dismissal, which he expected was coming, Mr. Girrior very foolishly tendered his resignation. Now the Employees Provident Fund Act provides that any man who tenders his resignation cannot participate in the fund. Had Mr. Girrior waited and taken his dismissal for political reasons or on account of political partisanship, he would have been entitled to the amount he paid
into the fund for the whole 14 years and upwards without interest and less certain charges such as the fees of the medical examiner. Had he stayed in the government service a few months longer he would have been entitled to his pension, but he resigned before the specified period of 15 years had expired. Having tendered his resignation however it is held by the Provident Fund Association that he is not entitled to participate in that fund. The section of the Employees Provident Fund Act to which I refer is the following:
The following employees, notwithstanding anything in this Act, shall not participate in any of the benefits of the fund under this Act, nor he entitled to a refund of any portion of -the contributions made iby them to the fund, that is to say:
Those, except as in this Act provided, who voluntarily retire from the service. [DOT]
The Provident Fund Association has claimed that as * Mr. Girrior voluntarily retired from the service he cannot receive the amount which .he now claims, namely, the amount which he has paid in. But 1 submit, and I direct the attention of the minister to this fact; that although in form the resignation was voluntary yet, all the circumstances being considered, it was not a case of voluntary resignation at all. but a case of forced resignation as Mr. Girrior apprehended the situation. Mr. Girrior taking into consideration the fact that the other man had been appointed as foreman, and that he was submitted to this extra work, of walking to the end of the section before the beginning of his days work, which under the circumstances he eauld not perform, naturally concluded that this was a means of getting him out of the way. As he puts it himself: There are lots of ways of killing a d'og besides choking him with butter. Under the circumstances he very foolishly I think, tendered his resignation. I do not blame the department at all-in fact I do not attribute any blame to anybody as far as that is concerned-but Mr. Girrior thought that by offering his resignation and by making no fuss he could participate in the benefits of the employees fund. He thought that would strengthen his case and he would be all the more likely to receive the benefits to which he thought he was entitled by tendering his resignation, which under the circumstances I submit was not voluntary.
The matter has not come before the department in any way at all.
I believe that.

But I will get a re-
I port on the case.

I would like to get from the minister some information in regard to the method that is adopted in the case of dismissals. Are 'the dismissals made by the department, or by the board of commissioners? The appointments, I understand1, on the Intercolonial railway are made by the board. When a young man asked me to recommend him for an appointment, and I bad to send him to the board. He had to pass some test in regard to his health, his eyesight, his age, and a number of other matters, and then having proved satisfactory he was taken on trial, and everything having proved1 satisfactory he was finally appointed^ Now, the board having the power to appoint men, it would occur to me that it also ought to have the power of dismissing them as well.

When complaints are sent into the government, under the rules of the brotherhood, the men cannot be dismissed without an investigation. I am carrying out that procedure to the fullest extent and to show how lenient we have been on the Intercolonial I will state that on the 1st September on the government railways there were 11,473 employees. The number complained of is 77, dismissals ordered 20, suspensions 2, re-instatement 1, investigations asked for or ord'ered 60. Only 9 of the 20 dismissed men have so far asked for an investigation. On the canals there are about 4,000 -men employed. There have been 24 dismissals, 4 investigations, and the constituencies affected number 9. In every case where an investigation on the railways has been asked for, and in many cases where that was not done, an investigation has been ordered.
Do I understand then, that the board has nothing whatever to do with the complaints against employees?

Not as far as political complaints are concerned. The board has power to investigate other complaints, of which there have been quite a number. Some of these dismissals wrere based on other complaints rather than complaints of a political nature.
One of the main reasons for the appointment of this board was that the Intercolonial railway should be taken out of politics altogether, and we were all hoping that result would have been realized.
Oh no.
Oh yes. Would it not be better when political or other complaints are made against employees in the service that those complaints should be referred to the board, rather than to the department?
I do not think that would be a proper course, because it would be bringing the board into politics. Where the complaint is other than political the board does conduct an investigation.

It has also been represented to me that employees complained against were not allowed to have counsel at the investigation, that counsel were not permitted to take any pair in the examination, and that only such questions as the commissioner allowed were asked.
Through the commissioner.

The questions must all be asked1 through the commissioner, and it is in the discretion of the commissioner as to whether questions should be asked at all or not. I have also been informed that the commissioner refused to put certain questions, that were considered fair and right, to witnesses. I would like to know' on what ground tlie people who are complained against are refused the advice of a friend who is willing to attend or of counsel. It puts the employees in a very aw'kward' position, as they are not accustomed to these trials. It will be difficult for them to get fair-play unless there is some one there to assist them and .bring out the truth. Would the minister say w'hether it is true that instructions have been given to the commissioners that no person is allowed to assist the employee in connection with his defence.

I follow the rules laid down by the agreement, which states that a man against whom a charge is brought can take a friend with him, a brother employee. A*nd no order has been given that counsel shall not appear.
Air. A1ACDONALD. Early in the session I asked if a Air. John Fraser had been employed as inspector of round-house construction in Stellarton in my county. The minister said that this man was so employed on the recommendation of the gentleman who contested the riding with me. On the same day I was informed by the Postmaster General that this same John Fraser had been dismissed from the post office in Stellarton for defalcation in connection with the trust moneys in his hands as postmaster. Even after this fact was mentioned in this House, the minister permitted this man to remain in the employ of his department not merely until the, work of construction which he was employed to inspect was finished, but until some ten days ago when I directed his attention to the matter after I had visited my county and had found the work finished over a month ago, and this defaulter walking around the streets of the town drawing

$3 a day and doing absolutely nothing. It may be that the minister was not aware of these facts., and I trust he was not. I make these statements on my responsibility as a member of this House. Some of his under officials permitted this defaulter to continue as inspector of construction for a month after the work was done-
It is not done yet.
The minister said the other day that this man was dropped from the employment of the department on February 23.
That is true. The chairman of the Railway Board informs me that the work is not done yet.

What work is not yet done? I was there less than three weeks ago and the building was being utilised as part of the round-house. It may be that some little details remain to be finished, but the contractors have worked out their contract and gone back. Let me tell the minister that while this man was inspector of the building, he was employed in some small office in the town which took up practically all his time. He did not give his whole time to the work of inspecting. The people in my county know the facts, and many of the political friends of the hon. minister, knowing this man, were surprised to find that one of the first acts of the government in my county was to put this man in an office of semi-trust and keep him under pay long after there was any practical need for his services. This is deserving the attention of the minister, and I ask whether he will inquire into it. If not, we will have to deal with the matter in some other way. I would like an answer from the hon. gentleman.
Will the hon. gentleman please put the question again?
I have called the hon. gentleman's attention to tacts, and I ask him to inquire of people at Moncton and see what the facts are with regard to the case.

I did not know that this man had been dismissed from the Post Office Department when I employed him. I did find out what his qualifications were as clerk of works, I found that he had served his apprenticeship as a carpenter for four years, and, after working at his trade for ten years, until 1870, was appointed as foreman carpenter in the Black Diamond colliery, taking full charge of all the surface work and buildings. After 1876, he again took up the building trade and had charge of building stations and freight houses on the eastern extension railway from New Glasgow to Mulgrave. I understand that there never was an investigation, and1 I do not think it is proper to call him a defaulter, for nothing was proven. I must admit, however, that had I known the circumstances, I would not have appointed him as clerk of work. When I made the statement, that the work was not finished, I made it on the authority of the chairman of the board who claims that it is not finished yet. It was to have been finished in December, but the time was extended by order in council.

I would like to know where the hon. minister got this statement as to this man's qualifications. There is no use in anybody trying to make out that he had not a fair trial on the charges of defalcation. He resigned in order to avoid prosecution, and his friends came to my political friends to intercede and prevent action. There is nobody in the county of Pictou, in the vicinity where he lives, that does not know this. If he was engaged in all this great construction work, he has not been doing it for the last thirty years, for he has been doing nothing but living off the public wherever he could1 get an office or a little job of some kind. I would like the minister to ascertain when the work on this round-house actually stopped, also whether this man has been doing anything in relation to that work for the last month, and whether he has been employed in other work in the meantime and drawing salaries from two or three different sources within the last six weeks.

I desire to draw the attention of the minister to the matter that the Boards of Trade of Chatham and Newcastle have taken up with me and also with the Department of Railways for some time past the matter of improved railway service. The deputy minister, at any rate, is well aware of the matter I am going to refer to. The villages of Doaktown and Boiestown are about half way between two principal business towns on the Miramichi and Fredericton. Doaktown and Boiestown are about 35 to 50 miles west of Chatham and Newcastle. The way trains are run at the present time, Northumberland citizens are able to do their marketing in another county, namely, at Fredericton. They leave their home in the morning, go to Fredericton, do their business, and return at night. The people of Chatham and Newcastle consider it a grievance for this reason: If a man living in either Doaktown or Boiestown wishes to do business in Chatham of Newcastle, he cannot reach these towns over the Intercolonial without losing one day and two nights; while he can go to Fredericton and do his business and come back the same night, an equal number of miles. The Boards of Trade of Chatham and New-

castle ask that a train leave either Boies-town or Doaktown in the morning, and go ea3t to the business centre of the county. Chatham and Newcastle are located about half way of the extreme length of the county. But as I said, the Department of Railways have not been able thus far to meet the wishes of the people of Chatham and Newcastle. I am reminded by the Minister of Railways that there is a surplus on the year's operation of about $700,000. May I not ask him to consider if there is not some way by which the residents of Doaktown and Boiestown can use the railway to go east, either to Chatham or Newcastle in the morning, do their marketing in the shire town of their own county, and in the other commercial town of their own county, instead of having to go to the shire town of another county to do their business and return the same night. It seems to me that money would be well spent in giving the outlying districts increased accommodation. It was my privilege to draw the attention of parliament seven or eight years ago to the fact that the Intercolonial was the only trunk line passing through that portion of the province of New Brunswick, and a duty devolved upon the management to see that the outlying districts were given reasonable transportation facilities, which was along the line of building branch lines. I will be told that there is hardly any business for an extra train, and that the people are served by facilities granted them to go to Fredericton instead of going to the business centres of their own county. I want to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that this is a grievance of which the people of Chatham and Newcastle complain.
While I am on my feet, I. want to draw the attention of the minister to another matter. He will find in the records of his department a petition from the people on the north side of the Miramichi in the parish of Alnwick, where there is a large amount of fishing business done, praying that the minister will take into consideration the building of a branch line from Newcastle 'down towards Tracadie, or as far as Tabucintac, a distance of about 35 miles. I am in entire sympathy with the policy of the government in their decision to build branch lines, and thus to accommodate the people of the outlying districts, who at the present time are without railway facilities. I would like, therefore, if the minister would bear that matter in mind. That petition is in his department from the people of the county of Northumberland, who are looking for their turn to come in the near future to get a branch line.
While I aim on my feet I would like to take this opportunity of drawing the attention of the minister to another matter. It Mr. LOGGIE.
is urged by my bon, friends, and by the Board of Trade of Newcastle, that at the present time the deep water facilities are not what they ought to be. They ask that a crane be placed on the wharf at Newcastle, and that the Newcastle wharf be enlarged. I have no doubt we shall have the pleasure of a visit from the minister later on, and I am sure he will give these matters his favourable consideration. They have been before the department already, but thus far have not been put right. I think it is my duty to call his attention to these matters, and hope he will give-them his favourable consideration.

I have received visits from deputations from both Newcastle and Chatham; of course they want the railway to run a different way. The great difficulty has been that there are twTo roads, one on each side of the river. I think if we adopted one side alone we might give them-some relief. It is a matter that I intend to bring before the board. With reference to the wharf, Newcastle and Chatham have both had it. I have received a deputation from Chatham, and they feel' they should have it still. As to the branch line, I have not had time to consider whether it is properly placed, or desirable in the interest of the country. But I hope to give it consideration, later on.

My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) has asked for a branch line in his county from Newcastle to Nackawic. I think that a branch line should he extended not only as far as Neguac, but as far as Tracadie where it would join the Caraquet North Shore road. This Caraquet North Shore railway is one of the branches which the department is now thinking of taking over in a short time as a branch of the Intercolonial railway. It traverses the most prosperous and wealthy districts in the province of New Brunswick. It is a great lumbering district, and we have immense forests, the development of which has been very rapid recently. The products of that district have not been able to reach the market of the western provinces because they are handicapped by the 'extra freight they have to pay. The fisheries besides, are immense, and the traffic in that line has been, increasing rapidly year after year. I hope the minister will take into consideration the advisability of leaving no gap along that peninsula between the Bale des Chaleurs and Miramichi bay. That road should connect Bathurst and Newcastle. I am sure the hoard of management of the Intercolonail railway and the Deputy Minister of Railways also, must be acquainted with the possibilities of that route in large passenger and freight traffic. We have also Die mines at Bathurst, which are worked by people from the east of Gloucester

county. People are getting more and more prosperous, and therefore better able to bring traffic and earnings to the railway. I trust the Minister of Railways will look into that scheme in the expectation of assuming control of the Oaraquet and North Shore railway, which should be extended to Tracadie and Newcastle, there adjoining the Intercolonial railway.

I would like to say a word with reference to what the minister has said regarding the possibilities of removing the rails from one side of the river. I would like to remind the minister that that railway has been through for thirty or forty years and while the earnings are not very great, I am sure the people living alongside that river would consider it a very great breach of faith and a grievance should the rails be raised. The population, of course, is small.
Did I make the stat-ment that I was going to remove the rails?
No, but I thought you said you were going to consider it.
I said that I was considering closing one.

That is what I mean. I understood the minister to say that he was considering closing one of the railways on one side of the river, and I presume it will be the side of the river which is more sparsely settled and where the income would be less. That is why I wished to draw his attention to the fact that this railway has been through for thirty or forty years and that the residents will consider it a great grievance if the privileges that they have hitherto enjoyed are taken away from them. While we have a surplus, it seems to me that if there be a portion of the road which is not a paying piece we might very well, in the interest of the whole and in the interest of the people at large, consider the localities served by the portion of the railway whose earning power is hardly up to what you would like it to be. I would like the minister to bear in mind the fact that after these residents have had railway facilities for thirty or forty years they would find it a grievance if these facilities were taken away. Chatham and Newcastle each have railway facilities. If Chatham requires increased railway facilities, and she is getting them, that is no reason why Newcastle should not havd increased railway and terminal facilities in keeping with the trade requirements of the town. One town is on one side of_ the river and the other on the other side of the river ,and there is no reason _ why there should be any undue competition between these two towns. An expenditure for increased railway facilities at Chatham was agreed to two or three years ago but the improvements are not
quite completed. I am sure that the minister will go on and complete that work at an early day. The department now own a very nice piece of property in the largest town in the county of Northumberland. Miramichi district is the Liverpool of the north shore of New Brunswick. From the district of Miramichi many millions of deals are shipped annually and many hundred thousand dollars worth of fish are exported. If I am not transgressing I would say that Miramichi fishermen during the iast winter lost $30,000 in duty paid to Uncle Sam's treasury that might have been kept in the pockets of the fishermen.

While we are on the subject of the Intercolonial railway, might I call the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to the present condition of the railway built from Matapedia in the county of Bonaventure to Gaspe Basin? As my hon. friend knows there are two sections of the railway. There was first the Atlantic _ and Lake Superior, built from Matapedia to New Carlisle, about a hundred miles, and then a new company was formed which completed the railway from New Carlisle to Gaspe Basin. The second section of the railway, 102 miles, was completed this last fall. The inspection by an engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals remains to be made in order to entitle the company to the balance of their subsidy. As to that I have no doubt that when the inspection is made the minister will find that this second section of the road is of a high class, exceedingly well built and will certainly bean excellent line. What I wish to bring to the minister's attention more particularly is the condition in which the first section of the railway is at present. There have been two companies, the first the Atlantic and Lake Superior and the second the Atlantic, Quebec and Western. The construction of the Atlantic and Lake Superior railway began some thirty years ago and it is a poorly equipped railway. It is really in a very bad state, and this winter the road was somewhat crippled on account, first, of the snow blockade, and second, on account of the many dangers that travellers found in travelling on a poorly equipped road. My hon. friend is authorized by a statute passed here last session to take certain steps with regard to a railway in this condition and I think he would do well this spring to send his engineer to inspect the first hundred miles. I wish to address some observations upon the items of Halifax docks and wharfs, and increased terminal accommodation. I desire to impress upon the minister the necessity of extended terminal facilities and railway accommodation at Halifax. I do so because I fear that the minister, coming from Ontario, may not fully appreciate as yet the railway situation in the province of Nova Scotia so far as the Intercolonial railway is concerned. At the beginning of this parliament the minister made some remarks respecting the proposed extensions of the Intercolonial railway from Dartmouth to the Musquodoboit Valley and a proposed extension of the Intercolonial railway into the counties of Pictou and Guysborough which gave me the alarming impression that he was not too strongly inclined to extend these branches, because he was not sure then that they would be profitable. I suppose one could hardly blame him for taking that point of view. Later I was glad to hear the minister state in parliament that it was the policy of the government to carry out the contract which the late ministry made for the extension of the Intercolonial from Dartmouth to the Musquodoboit valley as far as Dean settlement as agreed by the late government and I congratulate the minister upon his decision in that respect.
There is a widespread feeling in Canada that by reason of the fact that Nova Scotia has had the enjoyment of a government owned and operated railway that the province has therefore had great advantage over other provinces in railway transportation. This assumption is open to very grave question, because if we once were to go back to the earlier history of transportation, and trace it down to the present time it is dif-

ficult to gay whether the province as a whole has benefited by having a government owned and operated railway rather than a company owned and operated railway. The fact that Nova Scotia has had the Intercolonial railway has doubtless been of some advantage, but it has also had its disadvantages. In that province the Intercolonial railway system pre-empted the very best traffic sections leaving the lean sections to be served by private companies assisted by Dominion and provincial subsidies. It is true there are many sections of the province that do not hold out great inducements to railway traffic, and consequently railway constructing in many sections of the province was long delayed or never begun. I have always taken the position that the Intercolonial railway being in that province as a government system, after having pre-empted the best railway territory, should serve at least some of the lean sections as well. I am not arguing that to-day in view of existing conditions, the government should abandon the ownership and operation of the Intercolonial railway, that would be too big a question to discuss here to-night hut I do say that the Intercolonial railway being the _ chief system in that province and having the major portion of the railway traffic, should go into the railway business to the fullest extent and to the utmost needs of the people of the province. If they fail to do so, I think we who represent that province would be justified in asking that the government transfer the operation of that road to other operators. I shall not however discuss this further to-night.
However, I trust that the government will take the view that being railway owners and operators in the province now, they are willing and anxious to extend the existing system and meet to the utmost of their ability the needs of the different sections of the province.
There is ample opportunity there for extensions and improvements which are necessary, and ultimately sound from a business view point, even if they did not hold out hope of immediate or substantial financial profits. But I rose particularly to discuss the matter of railway terminals at the port of Halifax, which to-day are not satisfactory to shippers, to importers or to local wants. The conditions there, so far ;as the present needs are concerned, are very much the same as they were ten or fifteen years ago. At that time the Intercolonial railway could hardly meet the traffic demands of the port; but those demands have grown to such an extent that to-day the terminal facilities are hardly adequate to meet the business which the railway finds there. During the winter of 1911, when transatlantic ships were sailing from Halifax to Great Britain, they were very much handicapped owing to their inability, in consequence of the congestion at the terminals, to discharge and receive freight with any degree of promptitude. Just another illustration of the congestion last year. In the month of February last there arrived at the port of Halifax a quantity of freight destined for a point in western Ontario, which was not moved from Halifax until late in the month of April, a delay of considerably over two months, owing to the fact that it was stored in a freight shed, and was covered later with other freight, and it was impossible to get it out before. In addition to the steamers now calling at the port of Halifax, many other steamers would call there during the present winter months were they able to secure facilities. I am not approaching this question in a fault-finding spirit. The Board of Trade and business men of Halifax have been repeatedly urging upon various governments the necessity o'f extended and improved terminal facilities. Improvements have been made, but there has always been a tendency to make the extensions of terminal facilities merely to suit the immediate needs, instead of making them upon some comprehensive plan that would meet the requirements of the port for a great number of years. indicates that the railway tonnage at that port is increasing very rapidly, and provision must be made for the future growth. Now, I would like to state to the minister what in my judgment is needed at the port of Halifax. He of course knows that a year or two ago a somewhat comprehensive plan was arrived at by the Department of Railways for extended and improved wharfs and piers. At present the port has in connection with the Intercolonial railway 9 wharfs or piers, 5 of which are at Deep Water, so-called, and four at Richmond. It is, I believe the intention of the Department of Railways to construct at Deep Water some four or five new piers to replace the old ones now existing; the new piers to be of course much more modern and larger, and capable of handling a greater quantity of traffic and in a very much shorter time. Pier No. 1, the contract for which was awarded in August or September last, is now under construction, and when completed will be one of the most modern and largest piers on the Atlantic coast, either in Canada or in the United States.
Pier No. 2 is intended for freight and passenger traffic. Now, I understand-and as the minister probably knows I have not had an opportunity of becoming very conversant with the details of terminals at the port of Halifax-that there is another pier to be constructed, which is No. 3, I believe on the proposed terminal plans of the port, and which is similar to the one now under construction. I am instructed by the business men "and by the Board of Trade of Halifax, that it is extremely urgent that tenders be immediately asked for the construction of this pier, because long before it is completed it will be impossible for the new pier No. 2, together with any of the existing wharfs, to handle the traffic which will then be at the port. I trust that the minister, whenever he finds himself at leisure or whenever he can possibly give the matter consideration, after the closing of parliament, will ask hiis officers to take this subject into consideration, and1 after he does I hope he will find himself justified, as I believe he will, in directing that tenders be asked foT this new pier No. 3 so that it will be carried to completion as quickly as possible. There is another matter which I believe is the settled policy of the department, and that is the erection of a new freight-shed at the port of Halifax, a matter which probably was brought to the minister's attention when he was at Halifax during the late autumn of last year. The present freight-shed is certainly inadequate, and I am further led to believe it was improperly located when originally Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
constructed. I understand a portion of land has been already procured on the upper side of Water street whereon to erect a new freight-shed, and I trust that the minister will order the construction of this freight-shed to be commenced as early as possible, for I can assure him that it is extremely urgent at the present time. There is a further matter to which I would like to draw the minister's notice. I do not know whether his attention has been called to the fact before or not, and it is this: that a portion of the Intercolonial from Halifax- to the town of Windsor, is under lease to the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company. The freight-shed which is used by the latter company lies close to the Intercolonial station at Halifax. For certain reasons, which are unnecessary for me to mention, the freight-shed used by the Dominion Atlantic railway is very inconveniently located. All traffic reaching the freight-shed must proceed down or up North street, which offers a very heavy grade, and which renders truckage very expensive indeed, and this handicaps very much the shippers and importers at Halifax in sending out or receiving freight by reason of tnis fact. I am not aware if the minister's attention has been drawn to this particular point, but it is certainly a matter which deserves the consideration of the department. The Intercolonial should afford a more adequate and convenient freight-shed for the Dominion Atlantic railway.
I wish to say in connection with the terminal facilities at the port of Halifax that some broad and comprehensive scheme of extension of the Intercolonial rails along the water-front must at once, or very soon, be taken into consideration. I would hardly venture' to say to the minister what f think should be done, because I can scarcely ask him to consider me an authority in that respect, and whatever judgment I may have regarding the matter is entirely due to a limited personal knowledge of _ the situation and to information which comes to me by contact with the business men of the city of Halifax. Possibly I may be more ambitious than some of them in what I think should be done in this respect. I would like to make the suggestion to the minister that he and his officers should take this matter up, and possibly it would be wise for him to take into consideration the suggestion to obtain other expert advice upon the matter and consider the whole question of the extension and improvement of terminals at this port. I believe that ultimately the whole of Upper and Lower Water streets, so called, should be expropriated. I do not think it would be necessary to demolish or remove at once the structures erected on

the properties which would be expropriated. The rentals furnished by these buildings or properties would probably yield sufficient to pay interest on the capital amount necessary for the expropriation. At any rate a great portion of Water street should be expropriated so that the rails may be extended farther south. I think it is quite clear that the upper side of Water street at least, and possibly the lower side as far as what is known as the Ordnance yard- possibly this description is not very intelligible to the minister who may not know the location-should be expropriated as quickly as possible. However, as I said, il do not wish to express any definite or fixed views upon this point. And even if I had any definite or fixed views to-night I would hardly venture to give them to the committee in a dogmatic or definite manner. I shall be quite satisfied and content if I have the promise of the minister that during the summer he will take into consideration the matter of the adoption of a comprehensive scheme for the extension and improvement of railway terminals at the port of Halifax, so that at the next session we may discuss the matter more carefully and at greater length. Another matter which possibly I should mention in connection with improved terminals at Halifax is: whether or not the Department of Railways should not obtain possession of, and occupy the present dockyard between Richmond and Deep Water, and which is now in the occupation of the Marine and Fisheries and Naval Departments. If that property could be secured it would afford a great deal of yardage room for the Intercolonial railway, and also give additional dockage room. The feeling prevails at the port of Halifax that this dockyard should be occupied by the Intercolonial railway, and not by the Marine and Fisheries and Naval Departments, and I think myself there is a preponderance of fact in favour of it. I think a suitable location might be obtained on other portions of Halifax harbour, on the Halifax or the Dartmouth side, which would be sufficiently adequate for the necessities of the two departments referred to. But even if the dockyard property was secured' by the railway, there is still necessity for the expropriation of a great deal of property along the waterfront at Halifax. And there is this to be remembered; that in Halifax as in a great many eastern towns and cities to-day, the values of property are rapidly increasing, and unless this is done in the near future there will very soon come a time when the Intercolonial railway and the country will find these terminal facilities so imperative and so necessary that they will be obliged to buy the necessary properties, and then at a very greatly enhanced cost. There is just one further mat-134}
ter to which I would like to call the minister's attention, and which I had intended referring to when a later item in his estimates was reached, namely, the vote in connection with the extension of the Halifax and Eastern railway out of Dartmouth.
I refer to the necessity of a bridge across Halifax harbour between Dartmouth and Halifax at a point called the Narrows, where once a bridge was in existence but which some fifteen or twenty years ago fell down and has never since been replaced. The physical conditions along the waterfront on Bedford Basin and Halifax harbour proper and where the Intercolonial railway rails are laid and approach the city, are such that it is extremely difficult to get the necessary room. On the west side of the railway there is high and rocky ground, and it is extremely expensive to increase yardage or track room on this account. With a bridge constructed across the harbour, I think there could be found considerable yard room on the Dartmouth side of the harbour besides affording additional shipping facilities. I urge the minister to make inquiry and investigation as to the cost of the construction of a bridge, not only for the reasons already given, but for the further reason that the contraction of the Halifax and Eastern railway from Dartmouth to Musquodoboit valley is now a reality, and it will not take very long to build that road. If no bridge is constructed across the harbour, it will be necessary for passengers to leave the railway at Dartmouth and take a ferry across to the city of Halifax, and it will be necessary to transfer freight in the same way, or let it get to the city of Halifax via Windsor Junction. I do not wish the minister to understand me as saying here to- ' night that this bridge should be built at once. I think that first we should ascertain the cost of the bridge, and the subject might with greater satisfaction be discussed later. I think there is to be found in the department a report upon the construction of this bridge; but I think that at least, during the coming summer the matter should be carefully investigated. If the minister would be good enough to undertake that this should be done, I should for the present be content with that. It will not mean a very great expenditure, and at the next session of parliament the matter can be discussed at greater length.
I wish to repeat that the chief purpose I had in rising was to impress upon the minister the imperative necessity of extended and improved terminal facilities at the port of Halifax, not only for the good of Halifax, but for the good of Canada. Physically and historically Halifax is the winter port of Canada on the Atlantic coast. It is destined to be the winter port if not the all the year round port, for the fastest transatlantic

steamship services from Europe to Canada. It is at least bound to be the winter port of the transatlantic steamship services by reason of the fact that these ships are now becoming so large that they will be bound to select Halifax as their port of call and departure; and I say this without intending any reflection upon the port of St. John or upon the harbour known as Country Harbour in the county of my hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair). The export and import traffic at the port of Halifax is bound to increase very much indeed, as one can safely predict when he contemplates the tremendous development going on in this country. And I submit that, regardless of the cost, I care not what it may be, it is the duty of the government to give to the Intercolonial railway and to the port of Halifax such terminal facilities as port trade conditions warrant to-day, and in the expanding future.

The Minister of Railways has made some excuses why that step was taken by the present administration.
