I may say further

He says,
-that although hon. gentlemen opposite have quoted a great number of figures, there are no statistics in the department which I preside over, to warrant us in going on with the construction of this railway now. I believe that before committing the country to any expenditure, we should be able to give the people a just reason for our action and we should see that the tax-payers of Canada get a fair return for the money expended, or at least sufficient to pay the interest on the capital.
I submit that these are pretty hard conditions. In business ventures, of course, that is the rule that people lay down; they do not want to invest their money in any venture unless it will pay and unless they get some return for their capital. But, I submit that this is not a rule that has been adopted in this country in the case of the assistance which has been given by parliament to transportation. We have been subsidising railways, we have been deepening rivers, we have been constructing canals at vast expense for the last forty years in Canada and this is the first time, I submit, that any Minister of Railways has laid down the principle that we will not give aid to transportation in Canada unless the money we invest will not only pay the running expenses of the road but the interest as well. That is the way in which a Jew would approach a question of finance, he wants to see interest coming, he wants to know, when he puts his dollar in that he is going to get something out. That is not the way in which this ques-

tion has been treated by previous Ministers of Railways or by previous adminis-. trations in this country. When I say that I want to prove what I say and can prove it. Every hon. gentleman here knows that we have spent enormous sums of money in aiding transportation. It is placed in the books at $400,000,000. What return are we getting for it? What return in interest are we getting for the enormous amount of money we gave the Canadian Pacific railway? What return are we getting for the hundred million dollars that we put into the canals largely in the province of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals? Why, sir, we have not only spent an enormous sum in transportation in Ontario Canals but after we did so we passed an order in council declaring the canals absolutely free. Bring along your ships, pass through the canals, we will open the gates for you, we will give you the facilities and we will not charge you a cent! That is the way the government of this country has been treating the transportation problem in the province that my hon. friend comes from. Absolutely free! A hundred million dollars invested in canals and no interest coming to the people of Canada. I am not objecting to this because it develops the trade of this country. That is not the only case 1 might give, for there is the Intercolonial railway itself upon which a very large sum has been expended. Does any one expect to get interest out of the Intercolonial railway? Such a proposition has never been put up before by any Minister of Railways in this country and this is the kind of excuse that should not have been made in this case. If it is right to give these facilities free in the canals, if it is right that we should have spent such enormous sums of money in deepening the St. Lawrence river, if it is right that we should have built the Intercolonial railway connecting the different provinces together, and if it is right that we should have made these enormous contributions to transportation without expecting any return, why stop when a branch line is asked for in the county of Guysborough to connect some 18,000 people who are in an isolated position and who have good trade to offer the road? Whv is it that this proposition is put up to them and they are told that unless the road that they propose to build will not only pay running expenses but interest on the money, they cannot get it?
I do not think that my hon. friend should have given such an excuse as that, and I think on consideration he will see the unfairness of his proposal. The present minister is himself making a number of proposals with reference to transportation throughout Canada. He proposes to build a car ferry to connect the government railway on Prince Edward Island with the Intercolonial railway on the mainland. That is a good proposal. It has always been a handicap to the people on the island that they have to tranship their freight from the cars on the island to the steamship and then back to the cars on the mainland, and if these transhipments can be avoided it would be a splendid thing for the province of Prince Edward Island. Does any hon. gentleman say that that shall not be done unless the people on the island can show it will pay running expenses and interest on the capital? If you put it on that basis you cannot confer this great benefit on Prince Edward Island. We all know that the Prince Edward Island railway has never yet had a surplus, but at the same time it furnishes a good deal of traffic to the main line and in that way helps the road.
My hon. friend knows that it will be many years before the Hudson Bay railway can be expected to pay running expenses, yet that does not prevent him from entering upon its construction. But he says to the people of my constituency: You cannot have this road unless it pays expenses and interest.
I believe that this Guysborough road would offer a large amount of traffic, that it would develop	a good trade.
There is timber enough along the line to keep the road busy for the first ten years.	This is a good timber
country, and a large part of the wood is hardwood which cannot be profitably floated down streams. It comes from England, Ireland, Denmark, Norway, and nearly every other northern European country, and every one of them would have still to pay $2 a barrel to send their mackerel to the Boston market, while the Nova Scotian will get it in free.
Do you not agree with the late administration's theory that the consumer pays the duty?

This is true not only of mackerel, but of codfish, haddock and every other kind of fish that we sell in the American market. I think hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia have good reason to complain of the omission of that very important piece of road for which provision was made by the late government.
They will have to be patient a little longer.

They have been patient for .a great many years. I can testify that they were pressing this matter foT <a great number of years, and finally it was agreed that the government would aid the St. John Valley road in this way, and these other

branch limes should be built. I hope my hom. friend will look into the matter -again, and see his .way clear to restore the items for the construction of branches in Nova Scotia which have been omitted.

Perhaps I did not understand the minister as to the assistance to be granted the St. John Valley. I am aware of the guarantee of bonds for $25,000 a mile for the road. iMy recollection is that the agreement that was arrived at between the late Minister of Railways and the provincial government of New Brunswick, in the month of July last, w.as to the effect that the govemmemt was to furnish aid to the extent of about $400,000 for bridges, anld the bonds for the balance of the bridges were to be guaranteed by the province. I now understand that the Federal govexnimienit guarantees the bonds for the whole million dollars for the bridges.
Yes.

Then the difference between that and the proposition of the late government is that we were not guaranteeing bonds for the bridges, but we were to give a substantial cash bonus, supposed to be one-third the estimated cost of the bridges. Then the provincial government were to provide an equal amount. I understand now that instead of giving ia cash subsidy this government agrees to guarantee the bonds.
Yes.

I asked the minister whether the terms would be available to the government of Nova Scotia. Do I understand it .is a question of the probable revenue of the road; that is, that that is the only question that will have to be considered ?
In that respect, yes. I know we are taking desperate chances at 40 and 60 per cent. I do not know that there is going to be anything in it for the Intercolonial railway. '
It is forty per cent of the gross earnings ?

Of the gross earnings. It makes a great deal of difference where that road will run, and whether it is possible to make both ends meet on the forty and sixty per cent basis. For the Intercolonial as a whole, it takes about ninety-five per cent of the revenue to meet running expenses. I would not like to commit myself to any definite proposition, but I would be glad to discuss any proposition the provincial government may have to make. I would rather encourage the building of roads- in that way than to see the federal government undertaking the whole responsibility of an enterprise to develop the natural resources of a province. I think that

the federal government should build what you might call trunk lines; but these branch lines in a province constructed .solely for the purpose cf developing natural resources, I would aid in the same manner as we are aiding the St. John Valley road.

The way we looked at the matter was this, that in all probability for a few years both governments might sustain some loss. We consider that the federal government would lose some money in operating on the 40 per [DOT]cent basis, but also the provincial government would incur some loss because until the earnings reached $2,500 per mile, the 40 per cent would not pay the interest and therefore for three or four years there might be a loss on the part of both governments. But I felt, and I think the late Minister of Railways and Canals felt, that when the earnings reached $2,500 or $3,000 per mile it would pay on a 40 per cent basis. The Canadian Pacific railway lease the Tobique Valley railway, they operate on a 40 per cent basis, and I am told that the results have been quite satisfactory.
Have they to provide anything for betterments ?
I do not know, but it is not unusual that we have companies operating on that basis.

When the minister comes before the committee again I desire and would like him to tell me as well as he can the particular purpose to which this vote in the estimates for the Sydney mines diversion will be devoted.

I will give all the details.
